analysis.one_liner: Cuts red tape and makes Medicare Advantage plans disclose how often they delay or deny care.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2024 with seven bipartisan cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never heard from again — no hearing, no vote, no floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets prior authorization in Medicare Advantage — the step where a private Medicare plan must sign off before covering a test, surgery, or service. It would require plans to run prior authorization through standardized electronic systems instead of fax machines and closed portals, publicly report how many requests they approve or deny, how long decisions take, and when they use artificial intelligence to decide, and let Medicare set stricter deadlines for answers. Plans would also have to share their approval criteria with doctors and, on request, with patients.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans who currently wait days or weeks for plan approval of care their doctors ordered, and the doctors who chase approvals by fax. The bill's main gain is speed and visibility: plans would have to answer faster, and patients and the public could finally see denial rates, appeal overturn rates, and AI use plan-by-plan on a public website.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage seniors and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Plans imposing prior authorization would have to use a standardized electronic system for requests and responses; faxes, proprietary portals, and electronic forms that don't meet federal standards wouldn't count [S2].

Plans would annually report to Medicare the list of services requiring prior approval, approval and denial rates, how often denials were overturned on appeal, average and median decision times, use of AI or algorithmic decision tools, and grievances related to prior authorization — published on a public CMS website at the individual plan level [S2].

Plans would have to disclose their coverage criteria to providers under contract and to enrollees on request, and the Secretary could set faster response deadlines than the current 72 hours, including 24-hour or real-time decisions for routinely approved services [S2].

Plans would adopt transparent prior authorization programs developed with input from enrollees and providers, review annually which services require prior approval, and could waive requirements for providers with strong track records [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurance companies bear the cost: building electronic prior authorization systems, compiling and auditing annual public reports, disclosing criteria, and answering faster. Some of those compliance costs could show up in plan premiums or reduced insurer margins. Small providers would also need to adopt new electronic workflows.

drawbacks.text: The bill regulates process, not outcomes: it does not limit what Medicare Advantage plans are allowed to deny, only how quickly and transparently they must deny. A plan could still deny the same care, just more visibly and electronically [S2].

Response deadlines are discretionary — the Secretary 'may establish' timeframes rather than a fixed statutory clock, and real-time decisions for routine services only take shape through later reports and rulemaking, so the tangible speed benefit depends on future agency action [S2].

The requirements only kick in for plans that impose prior authorization at all, phase in from 2026–2027, and add reporting and IT costs that insurers could pass to premiums; the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission and GAO studies come years after implementation [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real but modest by design: faster answers for routine cases and public visibility into denial and AI practices, without restricting plans' underlying authority to manage care. The main honest cost is administrative — insurers and providers building new systems — and the main honest limit is that a denial, disclosed or not, is still a denial. On balance it leans clearly toward patients' access over insurers' administrative convenience.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2024, and the committee never took it up — no markup, no vote — before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) introduced the bill on June 12, 2024, joined by six original cosponsors from both parties: Sens. Sinema (I), Thune (R), Brown (D), Cortez Masto (D), Collins (R), and Fischer (R) [S4, S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it stayed for the remainder of the Congress [S4].
No further action of any kind — hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor consideration — appears in the bill's action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off: they face no electronic prior authorization mandate, no public denial-rate reporting, and no disclosure of AI-driven decisions, and can continue deciding on fax and portal timelines. Seniors waiting on approvals gain nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: Nothing about the bill's death was partisan: its sponsors spanned both parties plus an Independent, and the obstruction came from a committee taking no action rather than any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would force plans to replace fax and closed-portal approvals with standardized electronic systems, publish plan-level denial, appeal, and AI-use statistics, and meet potentially 24-hour deadlines. Insurers profit from controlling when care is approved, so transparency and speed cut directly into their discretion, though some compliance costs could reach premiums.

Doctors currently submit prior authorizations by fax and per-plan portals; the bill mandates standardized electronic transmission, requires plans to share approval criteria and required documentation, and allows waivers for high-performing providers. Less paperwork and faster answers serve patients too.

industries.industry: Health IT and electronic prior authorization vendors
industries.note: By excluding faxes and nonconforming payer portals, the bill pushes plans toward standards-based electronic transactions the Secretary would define, creating a market for compliant prior authorization software.
